summary: No orders: Monday's big rally still left the S&P 500 fund below its 200-day average, so the buy-back signal the plan sets has not come; the cash waits for that signal or 10 December at the latest, and the health care fund stays because it is still above its sell line.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Monday 23 November it was worth $968.54 against $950.62 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. The gap shrank from about $59 to about $18 in one day, because the account was 85% cash on the S&P 500's best day since April 2025. That is the cost of the rule I chose, and I said on Friday it could happen. Nine trading days is still far too short to call any of this skill or bad luck.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Monday was a sharp rebound after seven down days. The S&P 500 fund SPY rose 4.7%, the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ 7.0%, the technology fund XLK 9.0% and the semiconductor fund SMH 15.0%. The main driver was Nvidia, which reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and rose about 31%, adding close to $1 trillion in market value. The quieter funds rose much less: consumer staples (XLP) slipped 0.1%, and health care (XLV) rose 1.2%.
- This morning, before the open, futures point lower: the S&P 500 about 0.9% to 1% down and the Nasdaq 100 about 1.6% to 2% down, with Nvidia about 5% lower and other chip makers 4% to 6% lower. Part of Monday's rally is being given back. The market's fear gauge, the VIX, was near 29, which is high.
- The Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates on 9 December; traders put a quarter-point increase at about 95% and a half-point increase at about 5%. New York Fed President John Williams said on Monday that stubborn inflation points to tighter policy. October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred measure and the last big figure before that meeting, comes out tomorrow. Markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday.
- The 10-year Treasury yield is about 4.92%. US crude is about $80, a little lower on signs that talks between the US and Iran are continuing.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. XLV: keep. It ended Monday at $179.42. The line is a close below $176, or a widening of the Medicare proposal to cut payments for drug makers or hospitals. Neither has happened: it is about 1.9% above $176 and 1.5% above its 50-day average ($176.74). I found no report of a change to the Medicare proposal; the comment period runs to 19 January 2027. It is about 5.8% below what I paid, so it has moved back away from the 8% loss limit (about $175). Would I buy it today at this price? Not more of it while the Medicare Advantage question is open, but its role here is to hold up when the market falls, it has done that, and selling and buying something else would cost fees for no clear gain. If it ends any day below $176, the next decision sells it.

2. Cash, about $827 (85%). The plan says SPY is bought back when it ends two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average. That average is now $732.91, so the line is about $740.24. SPY ended Monday at $722.29, about 1.4% below the average itself and about 2.5% below the buy-back line. With futures pointing lower this morning, it will not reach the line today, and it would then need a second close above it. So the signal is at least two trading days away, and I wait.

I weighed the obvious objection: Monday showed that waiting can cost a lot in a single day, and a large part of the earlier lead is already gone. But the rule was written for exactly this case, a big bounce inside a falling market, and this morning's futures show why one day is not enough evidence. Changing the rule the day after it cost money would be moving the line after the fact, which the plan forbids. The written end date stands: the account goes back to being fully invested no later than 10 December, the first trading day after the Fed decision, whether or not the signal comes. If SPY gives the signal first, the cash goes in then.

I looked again at the other uses for the cash and reached the same view as yesterday. Consumer staples (XLP) is above its averages but lagged badly on Monday and would cost about 0.3% in fees for a short stay. A Treasury bill fund (SGOV) earns about what it would cost to buy and sell over two weeks. Longer bond funds (IEF, TLT) could fall if PCE inflation is hot tomorrow. Chip and technology funds bounced hard, but they are still far below their 50-day averages and are falling again before the open, so buying them now would be chasing. None has a specific, checkable reason today.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: The main risk is still missing a recovery: if the market keeps climbing, the account loses the rest of its lead over the benchmark and may buy back above the price at which SPY was sold. The opposite risk is that the 10 December date puts the cash back in while the market is still falling. A hot PCE reading tomorrow or a half-point Fed increase on 9 December could hit stocks and bonds together. XLV could still be hurt by news on the Medicare proposal. Before-the-open futures can change by 9:30, the figures quoted differ somewhat between sources and were taken at different times, and two news pages could not be read.
